blocks.text: May I be permitted here, in passing, to put forward the following conjecture. Nidda 67b states: אתקין רב אידי בנרש למטבל ביומא דתמניא משום אריותא; the women were permitted to take the river bath by day because the אריותא were to be feared. The word is usually translated "lions", and Süskind (מקור חיים on Jore Dea §. 197, 19) reads outright אריה; but would the lion stay near a populous town, and is it less dangerous by day than at night? Moreover, the lion never attacks two people who are together (§. 114), and so the general rule regarding the time for taking the bath could have been satisfied by bringing along a second person. I believe that אריותא here means "river current", in which sense it often occurs in the Targumim and the Talmuds. Naresch lay on the slope of a mountain (see Raschi on Sota 10a); rivers in such places are usually fast-flowing, since the water there as a rule forms a fall, and so bathing in such a river, especially at night, may well have been dangerous for the inhabitants of Naresch, which is why they were permitted to bathe by day.
The bear-driver is called דוב של שושטה (Rabba Wajikra fol. 171a); the ass-driver, on the other hand, חמר (Keluboth 61b), the camel-driver גמל (ibid.).

Ascheri, on A. Sara 58b, cites a passage from the Jerusalem Talmud Chala C. 4, H. 10 (where, however, רובין is read), in which דובים is the figurative designation for scholars, or for Christian officials.
Cf. on the derivation of this word p. 102, note **.

From the Jerusalem Talmud (Nedarim C. 2, H. 3) it emerges that one swears falsely who asserts under oath that he has seen a mouse fly (עכבר פורח באויר), from which it may be concluded that the bat bears no name in the Semitic languages which, as in French and German, is compounded of "mouse" and a prefix.

Probably from בות "to spend the night", the same as לון, and the word denotes a nocturnal animal, like the bat, or an animal dwelling in the dark, like the mole (§. 135); Luzzatto (Kerem Chemed vol. 4, p. 138), however, wrongly translates the word by פחות "the lowliest", for which no basis whatsoever can be found. By קפופות in the poem communicated there, the vulture is probably meant; see §. 188 at the end.
Volucrum animal parit vespertilio tantum.
Ova gignentium nulli (sunt mammae) nec lac, nisi animal parienti, volucrum vespertilioni tantum.

The eyes may well be injured by arrows hostile to the hair, yet only smear the spot, once the hairs have vanished, with the blood of the bird that with trembling skin deceptively imitates wings for itself.
Aruch has numerous variants to this Talmudic passage, by which the natural-historical statements read substantially differently.
In the Jerusalem Talmud (Demai C. 1, fol. 22a) it is related that a mouse once swallowed a pearl.
Because of its shorter forefeet it is also called צעירה רגלים (Sulat for the 2nd Chanukah Sabbath s.v. אין מושיע), where it is mentioned alongside שפן (§. 142).
And this animal is also called חגם (Targum on Prov. 30, 26) and טפוא (see Appendix under the word).
Rappoport (Kerem Chemed vol. 4, p. 224) reads כְּוִי, formed from כְּוִיָּה, as צביה from צבי etc., and translates it as "birthmark", i.e., the animal recognizable by a mark.
The pl. רחלות is said even to deserve preference, see Chulin 137b; cf. Luzzatto: Prolegomini p. 98.

פלגם 1) from פלג "dividing", i.e., standing between כבש and איל; 2) פלג גם and פלג, on which Maimuni: עדר הגדר, which should probably read: עדר הגדול "a head grown large"; 3) Φάγιλος [Phagilos] "becoming edible" (cf. on the transposition of the letters §. 146); 4) Πάλλης [Pallēs] "youth". — נוקד in Hebrew "herdsman" (Amos 1, 1), and the young animal is probably so called because in the 13th month it is handed over to the herdsman as an independent head, taken from its mother. — פרכריגמא, Greek Παραχάραγμα [Paracharagma] "counterfeit coin", i.e., an object of incomplete value, and likewise the animal which in the 13th month possesses neither the value of the כבש nor that of the איל. — Many read פרכדיגמא, but the former reading is undoubtedly to be preferred.
One should read in particular the Tosephot Menacholh 87a. s.v. שגובהן and the Talmudic passage there in general.

Let it be noted here in passing that in the tractate Aboth de Rabbi Natan cap. 35, where it is related that the pilgrims to Jerusalem made gifts of the skins of the sacrifices to their hospitable hosts, it says: these received כבשים המצויירין שעורותיהן יפה בר' וה' סלעים "excellent (marked-out) sheep, whose fleece was worth four to five Selaim"; a gloss reads: כבשי מצרים "Egyptian sheep", and here we are probably to think of the long-tailed sheep.

For חיוי ברייתי (field animals, Chulin 43b) Aruch reads עיזי ברייתי "goats living outside", i.e., wild goats. ברחא is explained by the Jerusalem Talmud (B. Kama 7, c) as תיישא רבא. — On the Mamber goat see p. 31, note *.

David, while he was still a shepherd, first let the young kids go out and eat off the tips of the grasses; then the he-goats, which plucked the blades of grass, and finally the old goats, which ate the grass roots. (Midr. Jalkut Schim. part 2, fol. 115a). In this passage צאן denotes small cattle in general.
חובצא דעיזא (Rabba Echa fol. 60 c) means either goat butter or goat cheese.
כרכמיש is said to be compounded of כרך "city" and the Nom. pr. כמיש; see, however, on the insertion of the ם §. 394, note.
